Nothing to Lose

Teenagers Who Never Held the Vote Declined as Much as Those Who Lost It

Author
Affiliation

Linlin Feng

Shenzhen College of International Education

Abstract

German states set the voting age for their own elections, while the federal voting age is eighteen. Therefore, some teenagers in Schleswig-Holstein in 2017 could vote in the May state election but not the September federal election. Leininger et al. found that their external efficacy declined and interpreted this as harm from losing the vote. Yet they both lost a previously held right and were excluded from an election. This paper asks whether the decline reflected withdrawal or exclusion. Using the original authors’ published panel survey of 3,897 teenagers, I first reproduced their comparison between teenagers who lost the vote and those who kept it. I then made their appendix comparison with teenagers who had never been eligible the centre of the analysis. Difference-in-differences models compared each teenager with themselves over time and then compared these changes across groups. External efficacy declined by 0.208 points among teenagers who lost the vote relative to those who kept it, while the corresponding decline among teenagers who had never been eligible was 0.182 points. The estimated lost-versus-never difference was −0.026 points, with a 95 per cent confidence interval from −0.157 to +0.106. This interval rules out an additional withdrawal effect as large as the published decline, although it remains consistent with smaller effects. Because the never-eligible teenagers were younger and there was only one pre-election wave, age-related differences cannot be ruled out. The evidence therefore shows that exclusion fits the observed decline as well as withdrawal does, rather than proving that withdrawal has no effect. Studies of rights withdrawal should compare people who lose a right with people who never held it and interpret uncertain estimates through confidence intervals.

Show the code 
# Load tools to organise the data, draw figures, fit models, and print tables.
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(fixest)
library(knitr)

# Read the survey: each row is one teenager answering one survey wave.
# ext_eff means external efficacy; demsat means satisfaction with democracy.
# id identifies the teenager; status identifies their voting group.
# The |> symbol passes the result of one step into the next.
survey_data <- read.csv("data/panel.csv")

# Keep the first two waves for teenagers who answered both.
# filter selects rows; mutate adds post, which is 0 before the election and 1 after.
panel_sample <- survey_data |>
  filter(wave %in% c(1, 2), in_w2 == 1) |>
  mutate(post = as.integer(wave == 2))

# Count teenagers once, even though each answers twice.
# na.rm = TRUE leaves out missing answers when calculating averages.
number_of_panel_teenagers <- n_distinct(panel_sample$id)
number_of_wave1_teenagers <- n_distinct(survey_data$id[survey_data$wave == 1])
city_percentage <- 100 * mean(panel_sample$kreisfrei[panel_sample$wave == 1], na.rm = TRUE)


# Compare how efficacy changed across voting groups.
# The part after | accounts for stable personal differences and changes shared by all groups.
# ref chooses the comparison group: kept first, then never.
# cluster = ~id accounts for the two answers coming from the same teenager.
efficacy_model_kept_reference  <- feols(ext_eff ~ i(status, post, ref = "kept")  | id + wave,
                 cluster = ~id, data = panel_sample)
efficacy_model_never_reference <- feols(ext_eff ~ i(status, post, ref = "never") | id + wave,
                 cluster = ~id, data = panel_sample)

# Save each estimate and its standard error, a measure of uncertainty.
# The quoted name selects the comparison; column 4 holds its p-value.
# Negative estimates mean a larger decline than in the comparison group.
# Adding and subtracting 1.96 standard errors gives an approximate 95% confidence interval.
efficacy_lost_vs_kept   <- coef(efficacy_model_kept_reference)["status::lost:post"]
efficacy_lost_vs_kept_standard_error <- se(efficacy_model_kept_reference)["status::lost:post"]
efficacy_never_vs_kept  <- coef(efficacy_model_kept_reference)["status::never:post"]
efficacy_never_vs_kept_standard_error <- se(efficacy_model_kept_reference)["status::never:post"]
efficacy_lost_vs_never    <- coef(efficacy_model_never_reference)["status::lost:post"]
efficacy_lost_vs_never_standard_error <- se(efficacy_model_never_reference)["status::lost:post"]
efficacy_lost_vs_never_lower_limit <- efficacy_lost_vs_never - 1.96 * efficacy_lost_vs_never_standard_error
efficacy_lost_vs_never_upper_limit <- efficacy_lost_vs_never + 1.96 * efficacy_lost_vs_never_standard_error
efficacy_lost_vs_never_p_value  <- summary(efficacy_model_never_reference)$coeftable["status::lost:post", 4]

shared_decline_percentage <- 100 * efficacy_never_vs_kept / efficacy_lost_vs_kept   # share of the decline the never group also shows

# Calculate each group's average efficacy in each wave, leaving out missing answers.
# The standard error and confidence limits show uncertainty around each average.
# These averages are used in both figures below.
efficacy_means_by_group <- panel_sample |>
  filter(!is.na(ext_eff)) |>
  group_by(status, wave) |>
  summarise(
    mean_efficacy = mean(ext_eff),
    standard_error = sd(ext_eff) / sqrt(n()),
    lower_limit = mean_efficacy - 1.96 * standard_error,
    upper_limit = mean_efficacy + 1.96 * standard_error,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

efficacy_means_kept_and_lost <- efficacy_means_by_group |>
  filter(status != "never")

# Repeat the same comparisons for satisfaction with democracy.
satisfaction_model_kept_reference <- feols(demsat ~ i(status, post, ref = "kept") | id + wave,
                    cluster = ~id, data = panel_sample)
satisfaction_model_never_reference <- feols(demsat ~ i(status, post, ref = "never") | id + wave,
                     cluster = ~id, data = panel_sample)

satisfaction_lost_vs_kept <- coef(satisfaction_model_kept_reference)["status::lost:post"]
satisfaction_lost_vs_kept_standard_error <- se(satisfaction_model_kept_reference)["status::lost:post"]
satisfaction_lost_vs_kept_p_value <- summary(satisfaction_model_kept_reference)$coeftable["status::lost:post", 4]
satisfaction_never_vs_kept <- coef(satisfaction_model_kept_reference)["status::never:post"]
satisfaction_never_vs_kept_standard_error <- se(satisfaction_model_kept_reference)["status::never:post"]
satisfaction_never_vs_kept_p_value <- summary(satisfaction_model_kept_reference)$coeftable["status::never:post", 4]
satisfaction_lost_vs_never <- coef(satisfaction_model_never_reference)["status::lost:post"]
satisfaction_lost_vs_never_standard_error <- se(satisfaction_model_never_reference)["status::lost:post"]
satisfaction_lost_vs_never_p_value <- summary(satisfaction_model_never_reference)$coeftable["status::lost:post", 4]

# Keep the two excluded groups after the federal election to compare anger.
# lost is 1 for those who lost the vote and 0 for those who never had it.
# Convert distance from the birth-date cutoff from days to years.
anger_sample <- survey_data |>
  filter(wave == 2, status %in% c("lost", "never")) |>
  mutate(
    lost = as.integer(status == "lost"),
    years_from_cutoff = days_loss / 365.25
  )

# Fit four anger models: no adjustments, background only, age only, and both.
# Background includes gender, migration background, school track, and city residence.
# Each teenager appears once in these models.
anger_model_unadjusted <- lm(anger ~ lost, data = anger_sample)
anger_model_background <- lm(anger ~ lost + female + migration + abitur + kreisfrei,
               data = anger_sample)
anger_model_age <- lm(anger ~ lost + years_from_cutoff, data = anger_sample)
anger_model_age_and_background <- lm(
  anger ~ lost + years_from_cutoff + female + migration + abitur + kreisfrei,
  data = anger_sample
)

anger_unadjusted_difference <- summary(anger_model_unadjusted)$coefficients["lost", 1]
anger_age_adjusted_difference <- summary(anger_model_age)$coefficients["lost", 1]

# Calculate the share of Wave 1 respondents who returned for Wave 2.
# Include those who dropped out so the return rate describes the starting sample.
wave2_response_rate <- survey_data |>
  filter(wave == 1) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(in_w2, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(rate)

response_sample <- survey_data |>
  filter(wave == 1, status %in% c("kept", "lost")) |>
  mutate(lost = as.integer(status == "lost"))

# Compare the groups' chances of returning.
# The second model checks whether initial efficacy predicts return differently by group.
response_model_group <- lm(in_w2 ~ lost, data = response_sample)
response_model_interaction <- lm(in_w2 ~ lost * ext_eff, data = response_sample)

response_lost_vs_kept <- summary(response_model_group)$coefficients["lost", 1]
response_interaction <- summary(response_model_interaction)$coefficients["lost:ext_eff", 1]
response_interaction_standard_error <- summary(response_model_interaction)$coefficients["lost:ext_eff", 2]
response_interaction_p_value <- summary(response_model_interaction)$coefficients["lost:ext_eff", 4]
response_interaction_observations <- nobs(response_model_interaction)


# Compare average birth dates in the two excluded groups, omitting missing dates.
# A later birth date means a younger group; divide the gap in days by 365.25 for years.
birthdates_by_group <- panel_sample |>
  filter(wave == 2, status %in% c("lost", "never")) |>
  mutate(mean_birthdate = as.Date(birthdate)) |>
  filter(!is.na(mean_birthdate)) |>
  group_by(status) |>
  summarise(mean_birthdate = mean(mean_birthdate), .groups = "drop")

birthdate_gap_days  <- as.numeric(birthdates_by_group$mean_birthdate[birthdates_by_group$status == "never"] -
                            birthdates_by_group$mean_birthdate[birthdates_by_group$status == "lost"])
birthdate_gap_years <- birthdate_gap_days / 365.25

1 Introduction

Context

Lowering the voting age may influence more than whether young people participate in one election. Voting while still living at home and attending school may make participation more effective as school and parents could offer support, and help voting become a lasting habit, as discussed by Franklin 2004 and Leininger et al. 2023. This also raises a broader question: do young people trust political institutions because they possess formal political power, or because they feel that institutions listen to them?

Germany’s federal structure allows voting rights to change across elections. Its sixteen states set the rules for their own state and local elections, while the voting age for federal elections is eighteen under Article 38 of the Basic Law. Schleswig-Holstein therefore allowed sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds to vote in its state election on 7 May 2017, but those still under eighteen could not vote in the federal election on 24 September. The state rule remained unchanged, and by the May 2018 local elections all three groups in the survey were eligible again, as described by Leininger et al. 2023.

Leininger et al. 2023 found that teenagers who could vote in May but not September became less likely to believe that politicians listened to people like them. Compared with teenagers who remained eligible, their external political efficacy declined by about 0.218 points on a five-point scale. The authors interpreted this as evidence that losing the vote harmed young people’s political attitudes.

Research Question

In September 2017, these teenagers experienced two changes at the same time. A federal election took place without them, and a vote they had held in May was no longer available. Comparing them with teenagers who remained eligible combines these experiences: the groups differed both in whether they lost the vote and in whether they could participate in September. It therefore cannot show whether the decline resulted from withdrawal or from being excluded from the election. Would these teenagers look any different if they had never had the vote at all?

Importance

Suppose the harm comes from being left out of the federal election. Then the teenagers who lost the vote were no worse off than they would have been if Schleswig-Holstein had never lowered its state voting age, because exclusion is the normal position of everyone below the relevant voting age. Suppose instead that the harm comes from losing a right they previously held. Then introducing the vote in stages created an additional harm, suggesting that voting-age reform should cover different levels of elections together. The original authors interpreted their result in the second way, so distinguishing these explanations matters.

Methods and Data

I first reproduce the original comparison using the authors’ published panel survey of 3,897 teenagers. I focus on the first two waves and compare each respondent’s answer before and after the federal election.

I then add the teenagers who were too young to vote in either election. As Figure 2 shows, birth dates determine membership in the three groups and also reveal that the never-eligible teenagers were younger than those who lost the vote.

Finally, I compare the changes experienced by the two barred groups. Difference-in-differences asks whether one group changed more than another over the same period, while comparing each teenager only with their own earlier response.

Findings and Contribution

I reproduce the original estimate: external efficacy declined by 0.208 points among teenagers who lost the vote relative to those who kept it. Teenagers who had never been eligible declined by 0.182 points, leaving a lost-versus-never difference of only -0.026 points. The original study attributed the decline to losing the vote, but my comparison shows that simply being excluded from the federal election fits the same decline just as well. However, because the never-eligible group was about 1.23 years younger, I cannot establish that exclusion caused the change. The two age groups may have developed differently over the four months.

Structure of the Paper

Section 2 reviews earlier research on political support, youth participation and voting rules. Section 3 develops the exclusion and withdrawal explanations. Section 4 describes the survey, groups and outcomes, while Section 5 explains the comparisons. Section 6 reports the results, Section 7 examines their limitations, and Section 8 summarises the argument and its implications.

2 Literature Review

Political support

The study of political support starts with Easton 1975’s distinction between specific support for the current authorities and diffuse support for the political system as a whole. Norris 2011 also states that it is possible for people to lose confidence in politicians and institutions without rejecting democracy. Employing more rigorous methods than those used in earlier observational studies, Kelly et al. 2026 discover that the link between political trust and participation is weaker than previous beliefs. The importance of these distinctions lies in the fact that believing that politicians listen is different from believing that democracy works. External efficacy and satisfaction with democracy may thus change in different ways.

Why young people vote less

A second group of studies examines lower turnout among younger citizens. Franklin 2004 argues that the elections which people take part in when they first become eligible can largely influence their future participation since voting might eventually become a habit. According to Blais and Rubenson 2013, the fact that young people have a lower turnout is due to their weaker political interest and their diminished perception of voting as a civic duty. Smets 2016 demonstrates that both life-cycle and generational changes account for the reason why the difference in turnout between younger and older citizens has increased. Evidence from Austria also separates low turnout from an inability to make an informed choice. Wagner et al. 2012 find that voters under eighteen made choices of similar quality to those of older voters, even though their turnout was relatively low. Their study concerns participation among eligible young people; this paper asks how young people respond when an election excludes them.

Since the first elections can influence later participation, the experience of being allowed to vote and then losing that right may also affect the political attitudes of young people.

How voting rules shape who votes

A third body of research shows how electoral rules affect participation. Braconnier et al. 2017 show that the amount of effort needed to register stops some eligible citizens from voting. Fowler 2013 discovers that compulsory voting in Australia changed who voted, thereby affecting the election results and policy. Leininger et al. 2023 look at teenagers who took part in the Schleswig-Holstein state election in May 2017 but were not eligible to vote in the September federal election; their sense of external efficacy decreased in comparison to teenagers who remained eligible, a result which the authors see as a consequence of disenfranchisement. The studies mentioned indicate that voting rules can change who takes part in elections and may also influence political attitudes.

What is missing

To my knowledge, Leininger et al. present the only study of young people who have lost the right to vote. Nevertheless, losing the right to vote always occurs alongside exclusion; a teenager who has lost their voting eligibility is also unable to vote in the present election. In Table F.2 of their appendix, the authors compare teenagers who have lost the right to vote with those who have never been eligible at all; they find a small difference of −0.06 points in external efficacy and regard this as broadly in line with their argument although less precise. However, this comparison is given only as one of a number of robustness checks, while their conclusion still attributes the drop to having lost the vote. That is the gap this article addresses.

The paper does not present a new dataset or identify a previously unexamined comparison group since the teenagers who were never eligible were already part of Leininger et al.’s data and appendix. Rather, I make the comparison in the appendix between the lost and the never-eligible groups the main focus of the paper. By using the same teenagers’ responses both before and after the federal election, I compare each respondent with their earlier response and then look at how the responses changed between the two groups. Finally, I interpret the estimate through its confidence interval, distinguishing effects that are inconsistent with the data from smaller effects that the sample remains too imprecise to exclude.

3 Theory

Two explanations

Exclusion. Being ineligible to vote may result a decrease in external political efficacy since it suggests the message that the political system has not yet regarded a teenager as someone whose opinions should influence an election. This message stands regardless of whether or not the teenager had been eligible before. In September 2017, both those teenagers who had voted in May state election and those younger teenagers who had never been able to vote were excluded for the federal election. Therefore, it is possible that both groups would become less likely to think that politicians listen to young people like them seriously. If exclusion is the main mechanism, external efficacy should reduce by about the same amount in both groups.

Withdrawal. The teenagers who voted in May for the state election were ineligible in the September federal election as the federal voting age of eighteen applied under Article 38 of the Basic Law. From their point of view, they went from being included to being excluded. I expect this change will be particularly noticeable. Since losing a right one has previously exercised can give a stronger feeling of rejection than never having had it, because recent inclusion sets a clear standard against which to assess later exclusion. The external efficacy should decrease more among teenagers who lost their eligibility than among those who were never eligible in both elections.

The test

Hence, by comparing these two groups, the competing expectations are separated. Although both groups were excluded in September, only one of them had been eligible during the May state election. If there were a similar decline this would support the idea that exclusion was the cause; but if there was a greater decline among those who had previously been eligible this would serve as evidence of an extra withdrawal effect.

Causal framework

Show the code

# Draw the arrows and labels, and hide the axes.
ggplot() +

Figure 1 shows how birth date determines whether a teenager was old enough to vote in May and September and therefore whether they kept the vote, lost it, or never had it. Birth date also determines age, which may independently affect how political attitudes change and therefore complicates the comparison between the lost and never groups.

4 Data

The setting and the survey

I use the original data collected and published by Leininger et al. 2023. The researchers surveyed 3,897 teenagers in Schleswig-Holstein, Germany’s northernmost state. Sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds could vote in the state election on 7 May 2017, whereas the minimum voting age for the federal election on 24 September was eighteen. Wave 1 was conducted following the state election and before the federal election; Wave 2 was conducted after the federal election. My analysis uses the 1,900 teenagers who responded in both waves, giving two observations per person. The published dataset is the original study’s own anonymised deposit: names and addresses were removed. The only available geographical measure records whether a teenager lived in Kiel, Lübeck, Flensburg or Neumünster, the state’s four independent cities. This applies to 39 per cent of my estimating sample.

The three groups

The two voting-age rules divide the teenagers into three groups. Table 1 shows whether each group could participate in the May state election and the September federal election.

Show the code 
# Count each teenager once and put the counts in the same order as the table labels.
teenagers_per_group <- panel_sample |> filter(wave == 1) |> count(status)
eligibility_table <- data.frame(
  Group = c("Kept the vote", "Lost the vote", "Never had the vote"),
  `May eligibility` = c("Eligible", "Eligible", "Ineligible"),
  `September eligibility` = c("Eligible", "Ineligible", "Ineligible"),
  Teenagers = teenagers_per_group$n[match(c("kept", "lost", "never"), teenagers_per_group$status)],
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(eligibility_table)

The first group was eligible in both elections and therefore kept the vote. The second group was eligible in May but was too young for the federal election, so voting eligibility that had been available to them became unavailable in September. The third group was too young for both elections and therefore never held the vote.

Figure 2 shows the birth-date distribution of all 3,897 teenagers who completed Wave 1.

Show the code 
# Plot birth dates for all Wave 1 respondents in two-week groups.
# Dashed lines mark the two voting-eligibility cutoffs.
wave1_birthdates <- survey_data |> filter(wave == 1) |> mutate(birthdate = as.Date(birthdate))
ggplot(wave1_birthdates, aes(x = birthdate)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 14, fill = "#4C78A8", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(as.Date(c("1999-09-24", "2001-05-07"))),

  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +

The group that lost the vote is the largest because its birth-date range covers a longer period than those of the other two groups. At the 7 May 2001 cutoff, the classification changes from teenagers eligible in May to those who were too young, although the birth-date distribution itself remains broadly continuous.

The outcome

My main outcome is external political efficacy, meaning whether teenagers believe political institutions listen to people like them. In every wave, respondents indicated how strongly they agreed that “Politicians do not care what young people like me think.” Answers range from 1, strongly agree, to 5, strongly disagree. Because the statement is negative, a higher score means that the respondent feels more heard. I also examine satisfaction with democracy, measured in every wave on a five-point scale. Finally, the survey asked teenagers after each election how angry they felt about not being permitted to vote. I use the responses collected after the federal election.

5 Methods

The comparisons

I use difference-in-differences to compare how each group’s external efficacy changed between May and September 2017. I compared every respondent with their own earlier answer and then compare the size of these changes across groups. Individual fixed effects account for characteristics of each teenager that remain constant over time, while wave fixed effects account for changes experienced by all groups.

I make three comparisons. First, I compare teenagers who lost the vote with those who kept it, reproducing the original study. Second, I compare teenagers who were never eligible with those who kept the vote. Finally, I compare the first two estimates. Both barred groups were excluded from the federal election, but only one had previously voted. The difference between their changes therefore estimates whether losing previously held eligibility had an additional effect beyond exclusion alone.

Reading a null result

I interpret the final comparison using its estimate and 95 per cent confidence interval. The confidence interval shows the range of effects that remain reasonably consistent with the data. An interval containing zero does not prove that withdrawal had no effect; it may also mean that the sample is too imprecise to detect a smaller effect. As Rainey 2014 explains, a statistically insignificant estimate alone does not establish that an effect is negligible. Following this reasoning, I ask which sizes of withdrawal effect the interval can rule out. I use the published decline as a comparison point, rather than conducting a formal equivalence test with a pre-specified threshold.

This interpretation depends on the two barred groups having followed similar trends without the change in eligibility. However, the never-eligible teenagers were approximately 1.23 years younger, and only one pre-election wave is available, so I cannot test this assumption. Attrition is another limitation: about 49 per cent of respondents completed Wave 2, and teenagers who lost eligibility were 6.7 percentage points less likely to remain in the survey.

6 Findings

Replicating the original finding

I start by replicating the comparison reported by Leininger et al. 2023. As Figure 3 shows, external efficacy falls among the teenagers who lost the vote compared to those who retained it. I estimate this decline at 0.208 points on the five-point scale, which supported the original conclusion that losing the right to vote was linked to a reduced belief in the political system’s responsiveness. Thus, the replication succeeds.

Show the code 
# Connect the kept and lost groups' average scores; vertical bars show their 95% confidence intervals.
ggplot(efficacy_means_kept_and_lost, aes(x = wave, y = mean_efficacy, colour = status, group = status)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lower_limit, ymax = upper_limit)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("May 2017\nbefore", "September 2017\nafter")
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(kept = "#4C78A8", lost = "#C44E52", never = "#8C8C8C"),
    labels = c(kept = "Kept the vote", lost = "Lost the vote",
               never = "Never had the vote")
  ) +
  labs(y = "External efficacy, 1–5 scale", x = NULL, colour = NULL)

Adding the group that never had the vote

To find out whether the decline was attributed specifically to losing the vote, I tested a third group: teenagers who were too young to vote in either election. Figure 4 shows that these teenagers who were excluded in both elections also became less externally efficacious. The decline was 0.182 points relative to those who kept the vote, compared with 0.208 points among those who lost it. Roughly 88 per cent of the decline observed in the lost group therefore also appears among teenagers whose formal political status of exclusion did not change. They had no voting right taken away from them because they had never been invited to a polling station at all.

Show the code 
# Add the never-eligible group, keeping the same labels and colours.
ggplot(efficacy_means_by_group, aes(x = wave, y = mean_efficacy, colour = status, group = status)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lower_limit, ymax = upper_limit)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("May 2017\nbefore", "September 2017\nafter")
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(kept = "#4C78A8", lost = "#C44E52", never = "#8C8C8C"),
    labels = c(kept = "Kept the vote", lost = "Lost the vote",
               never = "Never had the vote")
  ) +
  labs(y = "External efficacy, 1–5 scale", x = NULL, colour = NULL)

The difference between the two groups

The comparison that tests for an additional withdrawal effect compares the teenagers who lost it against those who had never had it. The difference between their declines is -0.026 points. The 95 per cent confidence interval runs from -0.157 to +0.106, with p = 0.703, so the data are consistent both with no additional withdrawal effect and with a smaller effect that the sample is too imprecise to detect. The interval rules out the published effect of 0.208-point decline but not one half that size, so it does not establish whether withdrawal accounts for most of the original decline. This does not prove that the true effect is exactly zero, and Table 2 sets the three estimates side by side.

Show the code 
# Collect the three model comparisons into one table.

Other outcomes

Satisfaction changed by -0.126 points among teenagers who lost the vote relative to those who kept it; the standard error is 0.046, p = 0.006, while the never-eligible group changed by -0.023 points; the standard error is 0.055, p = 0.683. The lost-versus-never difference was -0.104 points; the standard error is 0.053, p = 0.052, a suggestive but uncertain pattern. The three comparisons are reported in Table 4 in the appendix. Because I examined this outcome after seeing the main result, it should be tested again in future research.

Teenagers who had lost the right to vote reported 0.424 points more anger than those who had never been eligible. After I accounted for birth date, the estimated difference fell to 0.078 points, suggesting that age may explain much of the raw gap. The full regressions are given in Table 5 in the appendix.

Summary of findings

The teenagers who lost the vote did become less externally efficacious, so the original decline is real. However, teenagers whose political status stayed the same through both elections declined almost as much. This pattern points to something experienced more broadly than the withdrawal of voting rights alone. Possible explanations include the federal election campaign, its result, the political situation in Germany in autumn 2017, or a normal shift in adolescents’ political attitudes over four months. The decline is real, and it cannot be blamed solely on losing the vote, because teenagers who had nothing to lose declined just as much.

7 Discussion

What the results show

The original findings is real since I successfully reproduce it. Teenagers who had lost the right to vote became less likely to think that politicians listened to people like them; yet those teenagers who had never been eligible to vote also showed almost the same degree of decline. It therefore follows that the original comparison between those who lost the vote and those who retained it cannot demonstrate that losing the vote caused this change. The decline might be explained without invoking a withdrawal effect, since merely being excluded from the federal election is fairly consistent with the result of the group being excluded in both elections. This does not mean that there is no effect from losing the vote. The confidence interval still permits a smaller withdrawal effect, although the sample is not precise enough to detect it.

What the results do not show

The first limitation is age. Teenagers in the never-eligible group were, on average, 1.23 years younger than those who lost the vote. Comparing each teenager with their own earlier response accounts for differences that remain stable over time, such as one group beginning with higher efficacy. It does not account for the possibility that fifteen-year-olds and sixteen-year-olds change differently over the same four months. In a longitudinal study, Eckstein et al. 2012 find that political engagement attitudes and willingness to participate develop during adolescence, with different patterns across school tracks. They examine different outcomes, but their findings give a reason to question whether teenagers of different ages would necessarily follow the same trend here. The anger analysis demonstrates why this matters: a large initial difference between the groups almost disappeared after birth date was taken into account. With only one survey wave before the federal election, I can identify this limitation but cannot solve it using these data.

Attrition leads to the second limitation: only about 49 per cent of the original respondents answered the second survey, and teenagers who had lost the vote were 6.7 percentage points less likely to remain. As a result, the teenagers who are included in my analysis are not an exact representation of those who started the survey. Those with higher levels of initial efficacy were generally more likely to remain, though this relationship did not differ in a statistically significant way between the groups that kept the vote and those that lost it. The interaction test is reported in Table 6.

Finally, the paper does not say whether it is a good idea to lower the voting age; instead it focuses on the more specific question of whether teenagers respond differently when they lose a vote they had previously held as compared to when they have never been eligible.

What would change the answer

A series of surveys carried out before the election would enable researchers to determine if the lost and never groups were already changing along similar paths. Moreover, evidence from another region where voting rights changed in stages would also indicate whether this pattern applies beyond Schleswig-Holstein.

8 Conclusion

Restating the argument

In May 2017, some teenagers in Schleswig-Holstein could vote in the state election but were too young to vote in the federal election in September. The original study found that their external efficacy declined relative to teenagers who remained eligible and interpreted this as a consequence of disenfranchisement. I reproduce that finding, but then compare these teenagers with those who were excluded from both elections. Because both barred groups declined by almost the same amount, the evidence does not show that losing a previously held vote by itself explains the original decline. However, the never-eligible group was younger, so I cannot prove that exclusion itself caused the shared decline. The age difference does not solve the original study’s problem: comparing the lost group only with teenagers who kept the vote still cannot show that withdrawal caused the decline.

Contribution

The original authors had already compared the lost and never-eligible groups in an appendix, but treated this as one of the robustness checks. I make that comparison central, compare each teenager with their own earlier response, and use the confidence interval to show which possible withdrawal effects the data can and cannot rule out.

Broader implications

For this research, I aim to investigate whether losing vote hurts. The harm caused by losing something requires comparison between people who lost it with people who never had it, rather than only with people who still possess it. For policy, the results weaken the claim that introducing voting rights in stages necessarily makes young people feel unheard by later withdrawing them, while showing that ordinary exclusion from elections also deserves attention.

Unresolved questions

Could losing the vote have a smaller effect that this survey was not precise enough to detect?

Would the suggestive decline in satisfaction with democracy appear again in other data?

Do younger teenagers’ political attitudes change over several months differently from those of older teenagers?

# Calculate Wave 1 averages for each voting group in the panel sample.

  arrange(match(status, c("kept", "lost", "never")))

AI Transparency Statement

Writing

I asked codex to draft and reorganise parts of the Theory, Literature Review, Data, Methods and Findings, and to suggest clearer wording. I reviewed and revised its suggestions so that the paper followed my research question and evidence.

Code

I used codex to transfer my revised Word text into Quarto, connect numerical results to the code, check the grading requirements, help fix R syntax, remove repeated calculations, format figures and tables, and implement the satisfaction, anger and attrition checks. I checked that the models used the correct comparisons and that the text matched the estimates produced by the code.

What is my own work

The research question, the decision to center the lost-versus-never comparison, and the interpretation of the confidence interval are the substantive argument of my paper. I decided which suggestions to use, checked the results, and take responsibility for the final paper.
